article.title: FLIPR 2026 Senate forecast
article.subtitle: Silver Bulletin's prediction for every Senate election in 2026.

extraction.summary: Final FLIPR 2026 Senate forecast landing page as of Nov. 3, 2026: 82.4 percent Democratic control (Deluxe), average 53 D-47 R. The text is short; the substance is in embedded tables captured in the PDF. These are polling averages with per-poll influence scores; tipping-point probabilities, the Voter Power Index and elasticity by state; a popular-vote-to-Senate-seats translation table; and a polls versus simple/fancy/blended fundamentals table. The last implies the blend weights simple and fancy fundamentals roughly equally (simple weight about 0.46 to 0.49).

findings.statement: Final FLIPR Deluxe Senate forecast on Nov. 3, 2026: 82.4 percent chance of Democratic control, average 53 D to 47 R, a 6-seat Democratic gain, with a seat distribution from 40,000 simulations and a shaded middle 80 percent. At 50-50 Republicans control via the vice president, and Democratic seats include aligned independents.

For each state, FLIPR reports a tipping-point probability, the chance that state decides Senate control, and a Voter Power Index, the relative likelihood that an individual voter there determines the winner of the chamber, along with elasticity. Final values: Texas tipping point 12 percent (VPI 1.0, elasticity 1.04), Maine 12 (VPI 12.0, 1.07), Ohio 11 (1.8, 1.02), Kansas 10 (6.7, 1.06), Michigan 10 (1.6, 1.00), Iowa 9 (4.6, 1.05), Minnesota 7 (2.1, 0.94), Alaska 7 (VPI 17.1, elasticity 1.27), New Hampshire 4 (4.6, 1.13).
findings.rationale: Small states have high voter power per voter.

findings.statement: FLIPR's final Senate translation from national popular vote to control: D+1-2: 7.2 percent Democratic, 48 seats; D+2-3: 16.9 percent, 49; D+3-4: 31.8 percent, 50; D+4-5: 50.1 percent, 50; D+5-6: 69.2 percent, 51; D+6-7: 83.4 percent, 52; D+7-8: 92.8 percent, 53; D+8-9: 97.2 percent, 54; D+10-11: 99.8 percent, 55; D+14-15: 57 seats. The Senate tipping point was about D+4.5.

The final Senate polls-versus-fundamentals table shows blended fundamentals that are almost exactly a 47/53 to 49/51 weighted average of simple and fancy fundamentals in every state where they differ. Examples: Alaska simple R+1.2, fancy R+5.2, blended R+3.3; Georgia D+6.0, D+17.8, D+12.1; Kansas R+7.8, R+1.3, R+4.4; Maine D+16.4, R+6.9, D+4.3; Massachusetts D+42.1, D+34.1, D+37.9. That implies a simple-fundamentals weight of about 0.46 to 0.49 for Senate races in 2026.
findings.rationale: Consistent with methodology saying simple fundamentals get almost half the weight.

findings.statement: Final Senate polls versus blended fundamentals show how far polls diverged: Kansas polls D+4.1 versus blended R+4.4; Florida polls R+6.1 versus blended R+0.0; Iowa D+1.1 versus R+0.0; Maine D+3.9 versus D+4.3; Michigan D+4.9 versus D+9.9; Louisiana R+4.0 versus R+10.7; Alaska D+3.1 versus R+3.3.

Race-level poll influence scores on the final Texas Senate average: NYT/Siena (1,215 LV) 2.51, AtlasIntel (1,678 adults) 2.01, Emerson (500 LV) 1.84, Trafalgar (a Republican-classified partisan pollster, 1,089 LV) 1.79, Research Co. (450 LV) 1.70, Quantus 1.22, YouGov (2,138 LV) 1.07, Beacon/Shaw (Oct 15-19) 1.04. Older and lower-rated polls get progressively less influence.

For ranked-choice contests, the most-competitive-races chart shows the average simulated margin after the final round, while the full-slate table shows first-round vote shares. Margin charts show 10th to 90th percentile intervals, covering 80 percent of outcomes.

FLIPR draws most election polls from the NYT poll database but collects generic ballot and congressional approval polls itself. It includes polls from a few pollsters the NYT excludes and excludes surveys from banned or non-scientific firms.
findings.evidence_quote: We also include polls from a few pollsters that The New York Times excludes from their database, and exclude surveys from firms we ban or that don’t meet our standards for being scientific surveys.
